title: When Accountability Makes Us Think
text:
Organizations often assume that making people answerable for their decisions will make those decisions better. In 1999 Jennifer Lerner and Philip Tetlock reviewed decades of experiments on accountability and found that the truth was more complicated.

Across the studies they examined, the effect of having to justify oneself depended on exactly how accountability worked. When people knew in advance what their audience thought, they tended to shift toward that view and tell the audience what it wanted to hear. When people had to justify a decision they had already made, they spent their effort defending it, and became more rigid. Accountability could even make some biases worse, by encouraging people to use every piece of information, including irrelevant information.

Accountability tended to produce careful, self-critical thinking under specific conditions. People had to know before they made up their minds that they would have to explain their reasoning, the audience's own views had to be unknown, and the audience had to be seen as well informed and interested in accuracy rather than in a particular outcome. Under those conditions, people considered more alternatives and anticipated more objections.
lesson: To get careful decisions, ask people to explain their reasoning before they decide, and do not reveal the answer you prefer.
source: Lerner, J. S., and Tetlock, P. E. (1999). Accounting for the effects of accountability. Psychological Bulletin, 125(2), 255-275.
